claim: Copper is an essential enzyme cofactor in bacteria.
source: Copper is an essential enzyme cofactor in bacteria, but excess copper is highly toxic.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about copper's role in bacteria.

claim: Excess copper is highly toxic to bacteria.
source: Copper is an essential enzyme cofactor in bacteria, but excess copper is highly toxic.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about copper toxicity.

claim: Bacteria can cope with copper stress by increasing copper resistance and initiating chemorepellent response.
source: Bacteria can cope with copper stress by increasing copper resistance and initiating chemorepellent response.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background knowledge about bacterial responses to copper.

claim: CsoR is a copper-binding repressor that interacts with CheA in Pseudomonas putida.
source: By screening proteins that interacted with the chemotaxis kinase CheA, we identified a copper-binding repressor CsoR that interacted with CheA in Pseudomonas putida.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the pull-down screening experiment described in the abstract and Results section.

claim: CsoR interacts with the HPT (P1), Dimer (P3), and HATPase_c (P4) domains of CheA.
source: CsoR interacted with the HPT (P1), Dimer (P3), and HATPase_c (P4) domains of CheA and inhibited CheA autophosphorylation, resulting in decreased chemotaxis.
evidence: This is supported by BTH assays with truncated CheA variants shown in Figure 3.

claim: CsoR inhibits CheA autophosphorylation.
source: CsoR interacted with the HPT (P1), Dimer (P3), and HATPase_c (P4) domains of CheA and inhibited CheA autophosphorylation, resulting in decreased chemotaxis.
evidence: This is demonstrated by phosphorylation assays using [32P]ATP[γP] shown in Figure 2c.

claim: CsoR inhibition of CheA autophosphorylation results in decreased chemotaxis.
source: CsoR interacted with the HPT (P1), Dimer (P3), and HATPase_c (P4) domains of CheA and inhibited CheA autophosphorylation, resulting in decreased chemotaxis.
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assays on semisolid plates shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Copper-binding of CsoR weakens its interaction with CheA.
source: The copper-binding of CsoR weakened its interaction with CheA, which relieved the inhibition of chemotaxis by CsoR.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MST and pull-down assays shown in Figure 5a and 5b.

claim: Copper-binding of CsoR relieves the inhibition of chemotaxis by CsoR.
source: The copper-binding of CsoR weakened its interaction with CheA, which relieved the inhibition of chemotaxis by CsoR.
evidence: This is supported by chemotaxis assays with copper shown in Figure 5d.

claim: CsoR binds to the promoter of copper-resistance genes to inhibit gene expression.
source: In addition, CsoR bound to the promoter of copper-resistance genes to inhibit gene expression, and copper-binding released CsoR from the promoter, leading to increased gene expression and copper resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA assays shown in Figure 4c and qRT-PCR data in Figure 4b.

claim: Copper-binding releases CsoR from the promoter of copper-resistance genes.
source: In addition, CsoR bound to the promoter of copper-resistance genes to inhibit gene expression, and copper-binding released CsoR from the promoter, leading to increased gene expression and copper resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated by EMSA assays with copper shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Copper-binding of CsoR leads to increased expression of copper-resistance genes.
source: In addition, CsoR bound to the promoter of copper-resistance genes to inhibit gene expression, and copper-binding released CsoR from the promoter, leading to increased gene expression and copper resistance.
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data showing increased gene expression in the presence of copper shown in Figure 4b.

claim: P. putida cells exhibit a chemorepellent response to copper in a CheA-dependent manner.
source: P. putida cells exhibited a chemorepellent response to copper in a CheA-dependent manner, and CsoR inhibited the chemorepellent response to copper.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemotaxis assays with copper gradients shown in Figure 6a and 6b, where ΔcheA mutants showed no chemotaxis.

claim: CsoR inhibits the chemorepellent response to copper.
source: P. putida cells exhibited a chemorepellent response to copper in a CheA-dependent manner, and CsoR inhibited the chemorepellent response to copper.
evidence: This is demonstrated by chemotaxis assays showing that CsoR overexpression increases RI values (weaker repellent response) in Figure 6b.

claim: The CheA-CsoR interaction exists in proteins from several other bacterial species.
source: Besides, the CheA-CsoR interaction also existed in proteins from several other bacterial species.
evidence: This is demonstrated by BTH assays with proteins from other species shown in Figure 7.

claim: Chemotaxis plays a vital role in bacterial exploration and adaptation to complex environments.
source: Chemotaxis plays a vital role in bacterial exploration and adaptation to complex environments (Zboralski and Filion, 2020; Boin et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The chemotaxis signaling pathway is extensively studied in E. coli and S. enterica serovar Typhimurium.
source: The chemotaxis signaling pathway is extensively studied in the enteric bacteria Escherichia coli and Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (Wadhams and Armitage, 2004; Porter et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In E. coli, the chemotaxis system consists of five MCPs and six core components.
source: In E. coli, the chemotaxis system consists of five methyl-accepting chemotaxis proteins (MCPs) and six core components (the kinase CheA, the response regulator CheY, the coupling protein CheW, the methylesterase CheB, the phosphatase CheZ, and the methyltransferase CheR).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the E. coli chemotaxis system.

claim: Methylated MCPs and CheW activate CheA autophosphorylation in response to decreased attractant or increased repellent.
source: In response to decreased attractant or increased repellent, methylated MCPs and the coupling protein CheW activate CheA autophosphorylation (Parkinson et al., 2015; Ortega et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CheA is a phosphodonor for CheY and CheB.
source: The phosphorylated CheA (CheA-P) is a phosphodonor for the response regulator CheY and the methylesterase CheB.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CheA function in chemotaxis.

claim: Phosphorylated CheY binds FliM and FliN of the motor-switch complex, resulting in bacteria tumbling.
source: After CheY accepts the phosphate group from CheA, it binds FliM and FliN of the motor-switch complex, resulting in a switch in the flagellar rotational direction and bacteria tumbling (Welch et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CheA is a five-domain enzyme central to the chemotaxis signaling pathway.
source: Among the bacterial chemotaxis system components, the kinase CheA is a five-domain enzyme central to the chemotaxis signaling pathway (Bilwes et al., 1999; Muok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P1 domain of CheA contains the phosphoryl-accepting histidine.
source: The P1 domain (HPT domain) contains the phosphoryl-accepting histidine that becomes phosphorylated, the P2 domain (CheY-binding domain) docks the response regulator proteins CheY and CheB, the P3 domain (Dimer domain) dimerizes the CheA protein, the P4 domain (HATPase_c domain) binds ATP and catalyzes phosphoryl transfer to the histidine residue on P1, and the P5 domain (CheW-binding domain) couples CheA to other chemotaxis components by binding both CheW and the chemoreceptors (Bilwes et al., 1999; Muok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P2 domain of CheA docks the response regulator proteins CheY and CheB.
source: The P1 domain (HPT domain) contains the phosphoryl-accepting histidine that becomes phosphorylated, the P2 domain (CheY-binding domain) docks the response regulator proteins CheY and CheB, the P3 domain (Dimer domain) dimerizes the CheA protein, the P4 domain (HATPase_c domain) binds ATP and catalyzes phosphoryl transfer to the histidine residue on P1, and the P5 domain (CheW-binding domain) couples CheA to other chemotaxis components by binding both CheW and the chemoreceptors (Bilwes et al., 1999; Muok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P3 domain of CheA dimerizes the CheA protein.
source: The P1 domain (HPT domain) contains the phosphoryl-accepting histidine that becomes phosphorylated, the P2 domain (CheY-binding domain) docks the response regulator proteins CheY and CheB, the P3 domain (Dimer domain) dimerizes the CheA protein, the P4 domain (HATPase_c domain) binds ATP and catalyzes phosphoryl transfer to the histidine residue on P1, and the P5 domain (CheW-binding domain) couples CheA to other chemotaxis components by binding both CheW and the chemoreceptors (Bilwes et al., 1999; Muok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P4 domain of CheA binds ATP and catalyzes phosphoryl transfer to the histidine residue on P1.
source: The P1 domain (HPT domain) contains the phosphoryl-accepting histidine that becomes phosphorylated, the P2 domain (CheY-binding domain) docks the response regulator proteins CheY and CheB, the P3 domain (Dimer domain) dimerizes the CheA protein, the P4 domain (HATPase_c domain) binds ATP and catalyzes phosphoryl transfer to the histidine residue on P1, and the P5 domain (CheW-binding domain) couples CheA to other chemotaxis components by binding both CheW and the chemoreceptors (Bilwes et al., 1999; Muok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The P5 domain of CheA couples CheA to other chemotaxis components by binding both CheW and the chemoreceptors.
source: The P1 domain (HPT domain) contains the phosphoryl-accepting histidine that becomes phosphorylated, the P2 domain (CheY-binding domain) docks the response regulator proteins CheY and CheB, the P3 domain (Dimer domain) dimerizes the CheA protein, the P4 domain (HATPase_c domain) binds ATP and catalyzes phosphoryl transfer to the histidine residue on P1, and the P5 domain (CheW-binding domain) couples CheA to other chemotaxis components by binding both CheW and the chemoreceptors (Bilwes et al., 1999; Muok et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In X. oryzae pv. oryzicola, CheA interacts with and phosphorylates VemR to regulate bacterial virulence, motility, and EPS production.
source: For example, in the plant pathogen Xanthomonas oryzae pv. oryzicola, CheA interacts with and phosphorylates the response regulator VemR to regulate bacterial virulence, motility, and EPS production (Cai et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In V. parahaemolyticus, ParP interacts with CheA and prevents its dissociation from chemotaxis signaling arrays.
source: In Vibrio parahaemolyticus, a polarly localized protein ParP interacts with CheA and prevents its dissociation from chemotaxis signaling arrays, facilitating proper chemotaxis and accurate inheritance of these macromolecular chemotactic machines (Ringgaard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In C. testosteroni, CheA interacts with and phosphorylates FlmD, resulting in decreased biofilm formation.
source: In Comamonas testosteroni, CheA interacts with and phosphorylates the response regulator FlmD, resulting in decreased biofilm formation (Huang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In A. brasilense, the kinase CheA from each chemotaxis signaling system physically interacts with the CheY response regulator of another system.
source: In Azospirillum brasilense with two chemotaxis signaling systems, the kinase CheA from each chemotaxis signaling system physically interacts with the CheY response regulator of another system (O'Neal et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In P. aeruginosa, CheA interacts with DipA to regulate its subcellular localization and activity.
source: In Pseudomonas aeruginosa, CheA interacts with the phosphodiesterase DipA to regulate its subcellular localization and activity, leading to individual cell heterogeneity and motility behavior diversity in bacterial populations (Kulasekara et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Copper is an essential cofactor for enzymes involved in respiration and photosynthesis.
source: In most living organisms, copper is an essential cofactor for enzymes involved in fundamental processes such as respiration and photosynthesis (Kim et al., 2008; Tsang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bacteria have several strategies to increase their resistance to copper.
source: However, copper also has toxic effects on cells, and bacteria have several strategies to increase their resistance to copper (Giachino and Waldron, 2020; Andrei et al., 2020; Hyre et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The direct bacterial response to copper involves sensing increased copper concentration by sensors.
source: The direct bacterial response associated with copper resistance is highly conserved and generally involves (a) sensing of the increased copper concentration by sensors, (b) activation of bespoke transcriptional networks, (c) overproduction of copper efflux pumps that secrete copper out of the cells, and (d) recruitment of copper-binding and copper-oxidizing proteins that prevent copper from interacting with cellular components (Novoa-Aponte et al., 2019; Öztürk et al., 2023; Roy et al., 2022; Zuily et al., 2022; Dennison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The direct bacterial response to copper involves activation of transcriptional networks.
source: The direct bacterial response associated with copper resistance is highly conserved and generally involves (a) sensing of the increased copper concentration by sensors, (b) activation of bespoke transcriptional networks, (c) overproduction of copper efflux pumps that secrete copper out of the cells, and (d) recruitment of copper-binding and copper-oxidizing proteins that prevent copper from interacting with cellular components (Novoa-Aponte et al., 2019; Öztürk et al., 2023; Roy et al., 2022; Zuily et al., 2022; Dennison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The direct bacterial response to copper involves overproduction of copper efflux pumps.
source: The direct bacterial response associated with copper resistance is highly conserved and generally involves (a) sensing of the increased copper concentration by sensors, (b) activation of bespoke transcriptional networks, (c) overproduction of copper efflux pumps that secrete copper out of the cells, and (d) recruitment of copper-binding and copper-oxidizing proteins that prevent copper from interacting with cellular components (Novoa-Aponte et al., 2019; Öztürk et al., 2023; Roy et al., 2022; Zuily et al., 2022; Dennison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The direct bacterial response to copper involves recruitment of copper-binding and copper-oxidizing proteins.
source: The direct bacterial response associated with copper resistance is highly conserved and generally involves (a) sensing of the increased copper concentration by sensors, (b) activation of bespoke transcriptional networks, (c) overproduction of copper efflux pumps that secrete copper out of the cells, and (d) recruitment of copper-binding and copper-oxidizing proteins that prevent copper from interacting with cellular components (Novoa-Aponte et al., 2019; Öztürk et al., 2023; Roy et al., 2022; Zuily et al., 2022; Dennison et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The genome of P. putida encodes a dozen proteins involved in copper resistance.
source: The genome of Pseudomonas putida was predicated to encode a dozen of proteins involved in copper resistance (Cánovas et al., 2003), including copper sensor proteins (CopS-I, CopS-II), P-type ATPases for copper efflux (CueA, CopA-I, CopA-II, CopB-I, and CopB-II), heavy-metal efflux complex components (CusA, CusB, CusC, and CusF).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Expression of copper resistance proteins in P. putida is regulated by CopR-I, CopR-II, and CueR.
source: Expression of these proteins were regulated by copper-responsive positive regulatory proteins (CopR-I, CopR-II, CueR; Adaikkalam and Swarup, 2002; Hofmann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CueR regulates the expression of genes implicated in cytoplasmic copper homeostasis in P. putida.
source: CueR regulated the expression of genes implicated in cytoplasmic copper homeostasis, whereas CopR controlled the expression of genes involved in maintaining periplasmic metal level (Quintana et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CopR controls the expression of genes involved in maintaining periplasmic metal level in P. putida.
source: CueR regulated the expression of genes implicated in cytoplasmic copper homeostasis, whereas CopR controlled the expression of genes involved in maintaining periplasmic metal level (Quintana et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: EPS in P. putida biofilms shows high affinity for copper.
source: Besides, extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) in P. putida biofilms showed high affinity for most heavy metals, including copper, thereby providing a protective barrier under copper stress (Fang et al., 2011; Lin et al., 2020; Lin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In C. crescentus, reactive oxygen species derived from cytoplasmic copper ions mediate bacterial chemotaxis to copper.
source: For example, in Caulobacter crescentus, the reactive oxygen species derived from cytoplasmic copper ions mediate the bacterial chemotaxis to copper, and a potential cytoplasmic MCP McpR regulates bacterial chemotaxis in response to cellular copper content, enabling bacteria to escape from copper-rich environment (Lawarée et al., 2016; Louis et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In C. crescentus, McpR regulates bacterial chemotaxis in response to cellular copper content.
source: For example, in Caulobacter crescentus, the reactive oxygen species derived from cytoplasmic copper ions mediate the bacterial chemotaxis to copper, and a potential cytoplasmic MCP McpR regulates bacterial chemotaxis in response to cellular copper content, enabling bacteria to escape from copper-rich environment (Lawarée et al., 2016; Louis et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 43 proteins showed significantly higher amount in the CheA-binding column than in the control column in the pull-down assay.
source: In MS analysis, 43 proteins showed a significantly higher amount in the CheA-binding column than in the control column (Log2(fold change)>2) (Figure 1b, Supplementary file 1a).
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis of pull-down samples shown in Figure 1b.

claim: CheA showed the highest amount in the pull-down assay with a Log2(fold change) value close to 8.
source: As expected, the 'bait' protein CheA showed the highest amount, with a Log2(fold change) value close to 8.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: CheY and CheZ showed high Log2(fold change) values in the pull-down assay.
source: Meanwhile, the response regulator CheY and the phosphatase CheZ (two proteins known to be associated with CheA) also showed high Log2(fold change) values.
evidence: This is based on mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 1b.

claim: 19 proteins showed apparent interaction with CheA in the BTH assay.
source: The results from the BTH assay revealed that 19 proteins showed apparent interaction with CheA, including PP_2969 (CsoR), PP_1612 (Eno), PP_4111 (FusB), PP_5046 (GlnA), PP_1074 (GlpR), PP_4728 (GrpE), PP_0853 (IspG), PP_1877 (MsrC), PP_2378 (NfuA), PP_1023 (Pgl), PP_5006 (PhaD), PP_0691 (ProB), PP_0148, PP_1644, PP_2683, PP_3177, PP_3227, PP_3501, and PP_4460 (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is based on BTH assay results shown in Figure 1c.

claim: 16 proteins displayed obvious interaction with CheA in the BiFC assay.
source: The results displayed that except three proteins (PP_2683, PP_3227, and PP_4460) showed no apparent interaction with CheA, the other 16 proteins displayed obvious interaction with CheA in the BiFC assay (Figure 1d, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on BiFC assay results shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Five CheA-interacting proteins (CsoR, IspG, NfuA, PhaD, and PP_1644) inhibited chemotaxis in P. putida.
source: As shown in Figure 2a, five strains (WT +pcsoR, WT +pispG, WT +pnfuA, WT +pphaD, and WT +pPP_1644) displayed smaller colony than the control strain (WT +pVec), indicating a weaker chemotaxis ability in these five strains.
evidence: This is based on chemotaxis assays on semisolid plates shown in Figure 2a.

claim: No phosphate transfer happened between CheA and the 14 tested CheA-interacting proteins.
source: However, no labeling of the 14 target proteins was observed, and there was no apparent change in the phospholabeling of CheA after adding each of the 14 proteins (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a), suggesting no phosphate transfer happened between CheA and the 14 tested proteins.
evidence: This is based on phosphate transfer assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2a.

claim: CsoR and PhaD significantly decreased the phospholabeling of CheA.
source: As shown in Figure 2b, CsoR/PhaD significantly decreased the phospholabeling of CheA.
evidence: This is based on autophosphorylation assays shown in Figure 2b.

claim: CheA phospholabeling decreased as CsoR increased.
source: The results showed that CheA phospholabeling decreased as CsoR/PhaD increased.
evidence: This is based on autophosphorylation assays with increasing amounts of CsoR shown in Figure 2c.

claim: CheA phospholabeling decreased as PhaD increased.
source: The results showed that CheA phospholabeling decreased as CsoR/PhaD increased.
evidence: This is based on autophosphorylation assays with increasing amounts of PhaD shown in Figure 2d.

claim: CsoR and PhaD have no ATPase activity.
source: Meanwhile, the addition of CsoR/PhaD exhibited no apparent influence on ATP level as the addition of BSA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2b), suggesting that CsoR and PhaD had no ATPase activity.
evidence: This is based on ATPase activity assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2b.

claim: CsoR and PhaD have no apparent influence on the phosphate transfer between CheA and CheY.
source: The results revealed that CheA phospholabeling in the CsoR/PhaD-adding group reduced to a similar level as that in the group without CsoR/PhaD (Figure 2—figure supplement 2c), implying that CsoR/PhaD had no apparent influence on the phosphate transfer between CheA and CheY.
evidence: This is based on transphosphorylation assays shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2c.

claim: Three truncated CheAs (CheAΔHPT, CheAΔDim, and CheAΔHATPase) showed no interaction with CsoR and PhaD.
source: The results revealed that three truncated CheAs (CheAΔHPT, CheAΔDim, and CheAΔHATPase) showed no interaction with CsoR and PhaD.
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with truncated CheA variants shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: Two truncated CheAs (CheAΔYB and CheAΔWB) interacted with CsoR and PhaD with similar intensity as wild-type CheA.
source: In comparison, the other two truncated CheAs (CheAΔYB and CheAΔWB) interacted with CsoR and PhaD with a similar intensity as the wild-type CheA did (Figure 3b and c), indicating that the HPT (P1), Dimer (P3), and HATPase_c (P4) domains were essential for interacting with CsoR and PhaD, while the YB (P2) and WB (P5) domains were not required to interact with CsoR and PhaD.
evidence: This is based on BTH assays shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: The Dimer domain of CheA interacted with CsoR and PhaD like the whole-length CheA.
source: The result showed that the Dimer domain (DimCheA) interacted with CsoR and PhaD like the whole-length CheA did (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with individual CheA domains shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: The HPT domain and HATPase_c domain of CheA showed weaker interaction with CsoR and PhaD.
source: The HPT domain (HPTCheA) and the HATPase_c domain (HATPaseCheA) showed a weaker interaction with CsoR and PhaD.
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with individual CheA domains shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: The YB domain and WB domain of CheA displayed no interaction with CsoR and PhaD.
source: Meanwhile, the YB domain (YBCheA) and the WB domain (WBCheA) displayed no interaction with CsoR and PhaD (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with individual CheA domains shown in Figure 3b and 3c.

claim: CsoR bound to Cu2+ with a Kd of 5.5±1.98 μM.
source: The results revealed that CsoR bound to three out of the six tested metal ions (Cu2+, Zn2+, Ni2+), and the binding to Cu2+ was the strongest with a calculated binding constant (Kd) of 5.5±1.98 μM.
evidence: This is based on MST assays shown in Figure 4a.

claim: CsoR bound to Ni2+ with a Kd of 125±38 μM.
source: In contrast, the binding to Ni2+/Zn2+ was weak (with Kd value of 125±38 μM and 253±42 μM, respectively) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on MST assays shown in Figure 4a.

claim: CsoR bound to Zn2+ with a Kd of 253±42 μM.
source: In contrast, the binding to Ni2+/Zn2+ was weak (with Kd value of 125±38 μM and 253±42 μM, respectively) (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on MST assays shown in Figure 4a.

claim: CsoR showed no apparent binding to Co2+, Cd2+, or Mg2+.
source: Meanwhile, CsoR showed no apparent binding to Co2+/Cd2+/Mg2+ under the same condition (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is based on MST assays shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Deletion of csoR led to a weak but significant increase (about 1.3-fold) in the expression of copA-I, copA-II, and copB-II.
source: The results showed that csoR deletion (ΔcsoR +pVec) led to a weak but significant increase (about 1.3-fold) in the expression of the three genes, and complementation (ΔcsoR +pcsoR) decreased the expression of the three genes (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Addition of 10 μM CuCl2 induced about fivefold expression of copA-I, copA-II, and copB-II.
source: The addition of CuCl2 (final concentration 10 μM) induced the expression of the three genes (about fivefold; Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: CsoR is not required for copper-induced gene expression.
source: However, no noticeable difference in gene expression level was observed between WT +pVec and ΔcsoR +pVec, as well as between ΔcsoR +pVec and ΔcsoR +pcsoR (Figure 4b), implying that CsoR was not required for the copper-induced genes expression.
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: Deletion of cheA displayed no obvious effect on the expression of copA-I, copA-II, and copB-II in either the presence or absence of copper.
source: Besides, the deletion of cheA (ΔcheA +pVec) displayed no obvious effect on the expression of the three genes in either the presence or absence of copper (Figure 4b).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4b.

claim: CsoR represses the expression of nikB, cadA-I, cadA-III, cbtA, czcC-I, czcB-II, and PP_0026.
source: The results reveled that CsoR repressed the expression of nikB, cadA-I, cadA-III, cbtA, czcC-I, czcB-II, and PP_0026, and the inhibition degree was close to the inhibition degree of copper resistance genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: This is based on qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a.

claim: CsoR-DNA complex showed a stepwise increase with CsoR protein amount increasing from 5 to 20 μM.
source: The fragment of copA-I promoter exhibited a stepwise increase in the shifted DNA amount (CsoR-DNA complex), with the CsoR protein amount increasing from 5 to 20 μM (Figure 4c).
evidence: This is based on EMSA assays shown in Figure 4c.

claim: Adding Cu2+ to the reaction mixture decreased the CsoR-DNA complex.
source: Adding Cu2+ to the reaction mixture decreased the CsoR-DNA complex (Figure 4c), indicating that Cu2+ inhibited the interaction between CsoR and promoter DNA.
evidence: This is based on EMSA assays shown in Figure 4c.

claim: DTT enhanced the inhibition of Cu2+ on CsoR-DNA interaction.
source: As shown in the following Figure 4d, the addition of DTT (0.1 and 1 mM) decreased CsoR-DNA interaction in the presence of 0.2 mM Cu2+, and the addition of DTT alone had no apparent influence on CsoR-DNA interaction, indicating that DTT enhanced the inhibition of Cu2+ on CsoR-DNA interaction.
evidence: This is based on EMSA assays shown in Figure 4d.

claim: Cu+ converted from Cu2+ by DTT has stronger inhibitory effect than Cu2+ on CsoR-DNA interaction.
source: These results suggested that the Cu+ converted from Cu2+ by DTT had stronger inhibitory effect than Cu2+ on CsoR-DNA interaction, indicating that CsoR bound more strongly to Cu+ than to Cu2+.
evidence: This is inferred from EMSA results showing DTT enhancement of Cu2+ inhibition.

claim: Ni2+, Zn2+, and Cd2+ exhibited an inhibitory effect on the interaction between CsoR and promoter DNA, but to a much lower extent compared with Cu2+.
source: Besides, Ni2+, Zn2+, and Cd2+ also exhibited an inhibitory effect on the interaction between CsoR and promoter DNA, but to a much lower extent compared with Cu2+ (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on EMSA assays shown in Figure 4e.

claim: Co2+ and Mg2+ displayed no obvious effect on the CsoR-DNA interaction.
source: Meanwhile, Co2+ and Mg2+ displayed no obvious effect on the CsoR-DNA interaction (Figure 4e).
evidence: This is based on EMSA assays shown in Figure 4e.

claim: There was no significant difference between the growth of ΔcsoR/ΔcheA and WT strain at different copper concentrations.
source: However, in both cases, there was no significant difference between the growth trend of ΔcsoR/ΔcheA and the WT strain at different copper concentrations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c).
evidence: This is based on growth assays shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1b and c.

claim: CheA showed strong interaction with CsoR in the absence of Cu2+ with Kd = 0.17 ± 0.1 μM.
source: As revealed in Figure 5a, CheA showed strong interaction with CsoR in the absence of Cu2+ (Kd = 0.17 ± 0.1 μM), and the addition of Cu2+ (20 and 200 μM) led to increased binding constant (0.59±0.2 μM and 2.15±0.97 μM), indicating that copper decreased the interaction between CheA and CsoR.
evidence: This is based on MST assays shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Addition of 20 μM Cu2+ increased the CheA-CsoR binding constant to 0.59±0.2 μM.
source: As revealed in Figure 5a, CheA showed strong interaction with CsoR in the absence of Cu2+ (Kd = 0.17 ± 0.1 μM), and the addition of Cu2+ (20 and 200 μM) led to increased binding constant (0.59±0.2 μM and 2.15±0.97 μM), indicating that copper decreased the interaction between CheA and CsoR.
evidence: This is based on MST assays shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Addition of 200 μM Cu2+ increased the CheA-CsoR binding constant to 2.15±0.97 μM.
source: As revealed in Figure 5a, CheA showed strong interaction with CsoR in the absence of Cu2+ (Kd = 0.17 ± 0.1 μM), and the addition of Cu2+ (20 and 200 μM) led to increased binding constant (0.59±0.2 μM and 2.15±0.97 μM), indicating that copper decreased the interaction between CheA and CsoR.
evidence: This is based on MST assays shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The amount of CsoR bound by CheA gradually decreased with Cu2+ concentration increased from 2 to 20 μM.
source: A similar trend was observed in the pull-down assay, in which the amount of CsoR bound by CheA gradually decreased with the concentration of Cu2+ increased from 2 to 20 μM (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on pull-down assays shown in Figure 5b.

claim: The Cys69 residue of CsoR plays a critical positive role in copper-binding.
source: MST results showed that the CsoRC69A displayed significantly decreased copper-binding ability compared to wild-type CsoR. In contrast, CsoRC40A and CsoRH65A showed a slight decrease in copper-binding ability compared with that of the wild-type CsoR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1b), suggesting that the Cys69 residue of CsoR played a critical positive role in copper-binding.
evidence: This is based on MST assays with point-mutated CsoR shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b.

claim: The three point-mutated CsoRs (C40A, H65A, C69A) interacted with CheA with similar intensity to wild-type CsoR.
source: BTH assay revealed that the three point-mutated CsoRs interacted with CheA with a similar intensity to the wild-type CsoR (Figure 5—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: This is based on BTH assays shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e.

claim: Addition of Cu2+ significantly decreased the amount of CsoRC40A and CsoRH65A bound by CheA.
source: Results from the pull-down assay showed that the addition of Cu2+ significantly decreased the amount of CsoRC40A and CsoRH65A bound by CheA, but had less effect on the amount of CsoRC69A bound by CheA under the same condition (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on pull-down assays shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Addition of Cu2+ had less effect on the amount of CsoRC69A bound by CheA.
source: Results from the pull-down assay showed that the addition of Cu2+ significantly decreased the amount of CsoRC40A and CsoRH65A bound by CheA, but had less effect on the amount of CsoRC69A bound by CheA under the same condition (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is based on pull-down assays shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Adding CsoR and copper showed weaker inhibition on CheA autophosphorylation than CsoR alone.
source: CsoR alone significantly inhibited CheA autophosphorylation, while adding CsoR and copper showed weaker inhibition on CheA autophosphorylation (Figure 5c).
evidence: This is based on autophosphorylation assays shown in Figure 5c.

claim: CsoRC69A showed similar inhibitory effects on CheA autophosphorylation in the presence and absence of Cu2+.
source: Besides, CsoRC69A showed similar inhibitory effects on CheA autophosphorylation in the presence and absence of Cu2+ (Figure 5c), indicating that binding with CsoR was the prerequisite for Cu2+ to relieve the inhibition of CsoR on CheA autophosphorylation.
evidence: This is based on autophosphorylation assays shown in Figure 5c.

claim: In the absence of Cu2+, overexpression of point-mutated CsoR (CsoRC40A/CsoRH65A/CsoRC69A) led to about 40% decrease in chemotaxis.
source: As shown in Figure 5d, in the absence of Cu2+, the overexpression of point-mutated CsoR (CsoRC40A/CsoRH65A/CsoRC69A) led to a similar decrease (about 40%) in chemotaxis as the overexpression of wild-type CsoR.
evidence: This is based on chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 5d.

claim: In the presence of 200 μM Cu2+, the inhibitory effect of CsoR/CsoRC40A/CsoRH65A overexpression on chemotaxis was about 20%.
source: In comparison, in the presence of 200 μM Cu2+, the inhibitory effect of CsoR/CsoRC40A/CsoRH65A overexpression on chemotaxis was weaker (about 20%).
evidence: This is based on chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The inhibitory effect of CsoRC69A overexpression on chemotaxis was not affected by Cu2+.
source: However, the inhibitory effect of CsoRC69A overexpression on chemotaxis was not affected by Cu2+ (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is based on chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 5d.

claim: All tested P. putida strains showed chemorepellent response to CuCl2.
source: As shown in Figure 6a, the swimming zone of all tested strains was a circle shape in the control plate without CuCl2. However, all swimming zones showed an oval shape in the plate with CuCl2 gradient (Figure 6a), in which the bacterial movement distance near the plug (D1) was short, and the movement distance from the plug (D2) was long, indicating that the strains showed chemorepellent response to CuCl2.
evidence: This is based on chemotaxis assays with copper gradients shown in Figure 6a.

claim: WT +pcsoR displayed a higher RI value (0.428±0.015) than WT + pVec (0.373±0.021).
source: The results showed that WT +pcsoR displayed a higher RI value (0.428±0.015) than WT + pVec (0.373±0.021; Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on RI value calculations from chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 6b.

claim: ΔcsoR + pVec showed a lower RI value (0.324±0.013) than WT + pVec.
source: Meanwhile, ΔcsoR + pVec showed a lower RI value (0.324±0.013) than WT + pVec, and complementation increased the RI value to wild-type level (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is based on RI value calculations from chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 6b.

claim: Both ΔcheA +pVec and ΔcsoRΔcheA + pVec displayed no chemotaxis ability in either the presence or absence of copper gradient.
source: Besides, both cheA deletion mutant (ΔcheA +pVec) and cheA csoR double deletion mutant (ΔcsoRΔcheA + pVec) displayed no chemotaxis ability in either the presence or absence of copper gradient (Figure 6a and b), indicating that CsoR inhibited chemotaxis ability in a CheA-dependent manner.
evidence: This is based on chemotaxis assays shown in Figure 6a and 6b.

claim: In the control group without Cu2+ gradient, cells of all tested strains swam randomly in all directions.
source: In the control group without chemokine (Cu2+ gradient), cells of all tested strains swam randomly in all directions (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy and cell-tracking analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: In the group with Cu2+ gradient, cells of WT + pVec, WT + pcsoR, ΔcsoR + pVec, and ΔcsoR + pcsoR migrated towards lower Cu2+ concentration.
source: In the group with chemokine (Cu2+ gradient), cells of WT + pVec, WT + pcsoR, ΔcsoR + pVec, and ΔcsoR + pcsoR migrated towards the lower concentration of Cu2+ (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy and cell-tracking analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Cells of ΔcheA + pVec and ΔcsoRΔcheA + pVec swam randomly in all directions in the presence of Cu2+ gradient.
source: In comparison, cells of ΔcheA + pVec and ΔcsoRΔcheA + pVec still swam randomly in all directions (Figure 6c), indicating that P. putida cells showed a chemorepellent response to Cu2+ in a CheA-dependent manner.
evidence: This is based on time-lapse microscopy and cell-tracking analysis shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The center of mass value of WT +pcsoR (13.85±1.92 μm) was smaller than that of WT + pVec (21.77±3.60 μm).
source: The center of mass value of WT +pcsoR (13.85±1.92 μm) was smaller than that of WT + pVec (21.77±3.60 μm; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is based on center of mass calculations from cell-tracking analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: The center of mass value of ΔcsoR + pcsoR (14.16±1.41 μm) was smaller than that of ΔcsoR +pVec (21.39±2.02 μm).
source: Meanwhile, the center of mass value of ΔcsoR + pcsoR (14.16±1.41 μm) was smaller than that of ΔcsoR +pVec (21.39±2.02 μm; Figure 6d), suggesting that CsoR inhibited bacterial chemorepellent response to Cu2+.
evidence: This is based on center of mass calculations from cell-tracking analysis shown in Figure 6d.

claim: CsoR has no evident influence on bacterial migration speed.
source: The velocities (cell migration speeds) of cells from WT +pcsoR, ΔcsoR + pVec, and ΔcsoR + pcsoR were similar to that from WT + pVec both in the presence and absence of Cu2+ gradient, implying that CsoR had no evident influence on bacterial migration speed.
evidence: This is based on velocity analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The velocities of cells from ΔcheA + pVec and ΔcsoRΔcheA + pVec were lower than that from WT +pVec.
source: In contrast, the velocities of cells from ΔcheA + pVec and ΔcsoRΔcheA + pVec were lower than that from WT +pVec (Figure 6e), indicating that CheA played a positive role in bacterial migration speed.
evidence: This is based on velocity analysis shown in Figure 6e.

claim: The CheA-CsoR interaction exists between proteins from A. caldus, B. subtilis, P. syringae, and P. stutzeri.
source: The result showed that the CheA-CsoR interaction existed between proteins from A. caldus, B. subtilis, P. syringae, and P. stutzeri (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with proteins from other species shown in Figure 7.

claim: CheA and CsoR from B. diazoefficiens, L. monocytogenes, and P. fluorescens showed no apparent interaction.
source: However, CheA and CsoR from B. diazoefficiens, L. monocytogenes, and P. fluorescens showed no apparent interaction (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with proteins from other species shown in Figure 7.

claim: The intensity of CheA-CsoR interaction was stronger between proteins from B. subtilis.
source: Besides, the intensity of CheA-CsoR interaction was more vigorous between the two proteins from B. subtilis, but weaker between that from A. caldus, P. syringae, and P. stutzeri (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with proteins from other species shown in Figure 7.

claim: The intensity of CheA-CsoR interaction was weaker between proteins from A. caldus, P. syringae, and P. stutzeri.
source: Besides, the intensity of CheA-CsoR interaction was more vigorous between the two proteins from B. subtilis, but weaker between that from A. caldus, P. syringae, and P. stutzeri (Figure 7).
evidence: This is based on BTH assays with proteins from other species shown in Figure 7.

claim: Under low copper levels, free CsoR forms tetramer and binds to promoters of copper-resistance genes.
source: As shown in Figure 8, under low copper levels, CsoR molecules exist mainly in none copper-binding status (free CsoR) in the cell, and the free CsoR forms tetramer and binds to promoters of copper-resistance genes (such as copA-I), leading to repressed gene transcription and copper resistance ability.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8, based on the experimental data.

claim: Under low copper levels, free CsoR interacts with CheA and inhibits its autophosphorylation.
source: Meanwhile, the free CsoR interacts with CheA and inhibits its autophosphorylation, decreasing bacterial chemotaxis ability.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8, based on the experimental data.

claim: Under high copper levels, copper-binding changes the conformation of the CsoR tetramer and releases CsoR from promoters.
source: Under high copper levels, more copper-binding CsoR molecules exist, and copper-binding changes the conformation of the CsoR tetramer and releases CsoR from promoters, leading to increased gene transcription and copper resistance.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8, based on the experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Under high copper levels, copper-binding of CsoR decreases the interaction between CsoR and CheA.
source: Besides, the copper-binding of CsoR decreases the interaction between CsoR and CheA, which relieves the inhibition of CsoR on CheA autophosphorylation, resulting in increased chemotaxis ability.
evidence: This is part of the proposed model shown in Figure 8, based on the experimental data.

claim: The expression of CsoR (also named MreA) was induced by cadmium, nickel, zinc, and cobalt.
source: Previous research revealed that the expression of CsoR (also named MreA) was induced by cadmium, nickel, zinc, and cobalt (Haritha et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The homolog of CsoR in M. tuberculosis binds to copper and regulates the expression of copper-resistance genes.
source: The homolog of CsoR in Mycobacterium tuberculosis binds to copper and regulates the expression of copper-resistance genes (Liu et al., 2007; Marcus et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PhaD is a TetR family transcriptional regulator that behaves as a carbon source-dependent activator of the pha cluster related to PHAs biosynthesis.
source: PhaD is a TetR family transcriptional regulator that behaves as a carbon source-dependent activator of the pha cluster related to polyhydroxyalkanoates (PHAs) biosynthesis (de Eugenio et al., 2010; Tarazona et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Bacterial PHAs are synthesized under unfavorable growth conditions in the presence of excess carbon sources.
source: Bacterial PHAs are isotactic polymers synthesized under unfavorable growth conditions in the presence of excess carbon sources.
evidence: This is established knowledge about PHAs.

claim: PHAs act as dynamic carbon reservoirs and reducing equivalents.
source: PHAs are critical in central metabolism, acting as dynamic carbon reservoirs and reducing equivalents (Gregory et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: PP_1644 is annotated as a NAD(P)H dehydrogenase involved in cyclic electron transport and respiration processes.
source: Another CheA-interacting protein, PP_1644, also attracts our interest. PP_1644 is annotated as a NAD(P)H dehydrogenase involved in cyclic electron transport and respiration processes.
evidence: This is based on annotation information.

claim: CsoR is annotated as a metal-binding transcriptional repressor.
source: Of the two proteins that inhibit CheA autophosphorylation, CsoR is annotated as a metal-binding transcriptional repressor, and PhaD is annotated as a TetR family transcriptional regulator (Winsor et al., 2016.)
evidence: This is based on annotation information supported by citation.

claim: PhaD is annotated as a TetR family transcriptional regulator.
source: Of the two proteins that inhibit CheA autophosphorylation, CsoR is annotated as a metal-binding transcriptional repressor, and PhaD is annotated as a TetR family transcriptional regulator (Winsor et al., 2016.)
evidence: This is based on annotation information supported by citation.

claim: CsoR and PhaD show no sequence similarity.
source: BLAST result revealed no sequence similarity between CsoR and PhaD (data not shown).
evidence: This is based on BLAST analysis.

claim: CsoR and PhaD show no significant structural similarity.
source: However, the result revealed no significant structural similarity between the two proteins (Figure 3—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison using Pymol shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1c.

claim: In M. tuberculosis, CsoR binds a single-monomer mole equivalent of Cu+ to form a trigonally coordinated complex.
source: Previous study in M. tuberculosis showed that CsoR bound a single-monomer mole equivalent of Cu+ to form a trigonally coordinated complex (Liu et al., 2007), but our results indicated that CsoR bound to Cu2+.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: DTT can reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ in solution.
source: DTT can reduce Cu2+ to Cu+ in solution (Krȩżel et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The role of CsoR in regulating copper resistance has been reported in several bacterial species.
source: The role of CsoR in regulating copper resistance has been reported in several bacterial species, including Acidithiobacillus caldus (Hou et al., 2021), Bacillus subtilis (Smaldone and Helmann, 2007), Bradyrhizobium diazoefficiens (Pacheco et al., 2023), Corynebacterium glutamicumTeramoto et al., 2015, Listeria monocytogenes (Corbett et al., 2011), M. tuberculosis (Marcus et al., 2016), Staphylococcus aureus (Baker et al., 2011), Streptomyces lividans (Dwarakanath et al., 2012), and Thermus thermophilus (Sakamoto et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In M. tuberculosis, B. subtilis, C. glutamicum, L. monocytogenes, and S. aureus, deletion of csoR resulted in about 10-fold increase in the expression of target genes in the absence of copper.
source: In M. tuberculosis, B. subtilis, C. glutamicum, L. monocytogenes, and S. aureus, deletion of csoR resulted in an about 10-fold increase in the expression of target genes in the absence of copper (Marcus et al., 2016; Smaldone and Helmann, 2007; Teramoto et al., 2015; Corbett et al., 2011; Baker et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CueR positively regulates the expression of cueA in P. putida.
source: CueR positively regulated the expression of cueA, encoding a copper-transporting P1-type ATPase that played a crucial role in copper resistance (Adaikkalam and Swarup, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CopR is essential for expressing copA-II, copB-II, and cusA in P. putida.
source: CopR was essential for expressing several genes implicated in cytoplasmic copper homeostasis, such as copA-II, copB-II, and cusA (Quintana et al., 2017; Quaranta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There is no CsoR homolog in P. aeruginosa.
source: Consistent with this, there is no CosR homolog in P. aeruginosa, and copper homeostasis in P. aeruginosa is mainly controlled by CueR and CopR (Hofmann et al., 2021; Quintana et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Copper homeostasis in P. aeruginosa is mainly controlled by CueR and CopR.
source: Consistent with this, there is no CosR homolog in P. aeruginosa, and copper homeostasis in P. aeruginosa is mainly controlled by CueR and CopR (Hofmann et al., 2021; Quintana et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.
